title:
"Is this AI?"
is the wrong
question.
sub: The one that actually decides your validation burden — and the four answers that settle it.

title: Ask "is this AI?" and you get a *definitional debate*.
text: Almost anything can be argued into or out of the label. And nothing about the answer tells you what validation you owe.

title:
The question that works:
*"What happens when it's wrong?"*
text: Regulators reason about consequence, not category. Your intake form should too.

title: What does the output touch?
text: A GxP decision, a GxP record, or neither. If it touches neither, you're documenting scope — not validating a system.

title: How much does it influence that decision?
text: Informational. Advisory. Direct. Autonomous. Influence is a dial — and it moves your obligation far more than the technology does.

title: Can it change on its own?
text: A locked model behaves tomorrow the way it behaved at qualification. An adaptive one — or a vendor-updated one — does not. That single difference is your entire monitoring burden.

title: What does the human actually do?
text: Reviews every output, samples them, or rubber-stamps them. "Human in the loop" isn't a control until you can say which — and show it works.

title:
Four answers.
One repeatable decision.
items: *Same inputs, same class* — whoever runs the form.
*Proportionate depth* — most low-risk uses clear in days, not quarters.
*A defensible record* — the reasoning survives "why this level?"
*A re-trigger* — re-run it when the model, the use, or the vendor changes.

title:
Governance isn't the brake.
*Not being able to decide* is.
text: If your AI projects are waiting on a framework, the bottleneck isn't risk appetite. It's the absence of a repeatable answer.
